h1: Collaboration brews: why breweries brew together
title: Collaboration Brews Explained | Craft Beer School
desc: What a collaboration brew is, why breweries make them and what each side gains, from shared recipes to new drinkers and a good story.
teaser: Two breweries, one brew day and a beer neither would have made alone. Here is why rivals do it.
standfirst: Collaboration brews are one of craft beer's oddest habits: competing breweries sharing a brewhouse, a recipe and a label. Here is how they work and why drinkers love them.
sections:
A collaboration brew, or collab, is a beer made by two or more breweries together. Usually one brewery hosts the brew day and the other team travels in. They design the recipe together, brew it on the host's kit and release it under both names, often with a label that blends both brands.

Sometimes the partner is not a brewery at all. Breweries collaborate with coffee roasters, chocolate makers, tea estates, restaurants, bakeries and even artists. The beer becomes a meeting point between two crafts.

From the outside it looks odd. Breweries compete for the same taps and the same drinkers. Yet collaboration has been part of craft beer culture for a long time. It grows from how small breweries actually work. Brewers learn from each other, share spare yeast or a bag of malt in an emergency and drink at each other's taprooms.

A collab also makes commercial sense. Each brewery introduces its partner to its own regulars. A drinker loyal to one brewery tries the other because the names are on the same can. For a new brewery, a collab with an established one can be the fastest way to be noticed. Our guide to craft beer in India describes how close the Indian scene is, which makes this kind of sharing natural.
What happens on a collab brew day

The visiting team usually arrives early, because brew days start early. The two head brewers agree the recipe in advance, often over weeks of messages: the style, the target gravity, the hops and any special ingredient. On the day, one team mills and mashes in while the other weighs hop additions and sets up the fermenter.

One practical detail always matters: the recipe has to be scaled to the host's brewhouse. A recipe built for a brewery getting 80% efficiency on its own kit may hit a lower or higher gravity on someone else's. Good brewers take a gravity reading after the mash and adjust before the boil rather than guessing.

The rest of the day is cleaning, talking and tasting each other's beers. Many brewers say the conversations are worth as much as the beer.

For drinkers, a collab is an event. It is usually a limited release, available for a few weeks, so it feels special. It often tries something neither brewery normally makes: an unusual ingredient, a different yeast or a style outside both ranges. And it comes with a story about two teams in a brewhouse together, which makes it easy to talk about.

Collabs are a good way into craft beer for curious drinkers. If you are new to the styles involved, our beer styles guide helps you read the label.

Not every collab works. The good ones share a few traits:

  • A reason. The partners bring something different, such as a local ingredient, a speciality or a skill.
  • Clear roles. Who brews, who packages, who sells, who handles the paperwork and how the beer is split.
  • A label both teams agree on. Both brands should be recognisable, with nobody's identity lost.
  • Honest marketing. The story should be what really happened, not an invented legend.

In India there is an extra layer. Moving beer, ingredients or even a brewing team between states can involve excise permissions. The rules on brewing a beer under another brand's name vary by state. Breweries planning a collab check the current position with their licensing adviser before agreeing anything.
Why collaborations are a branding skill

A collab looks like a brewing project but succeeds or fails as a branding one. Two visual identities have to share one label. Two sets of followers have to hear about it at the same time. The release has to feel special without confusing anyone about who makes your core beers.

Breweries that do this well treat each collab as a small campaign: a reason, a story, a label, a launch and a short window to try it. That same thinking applies to every seasonal and limited release a brewery makes.
